utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Madam Registrar, would you please call the case.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Case number IT-98-29-T, the Prosecutor versus Stanislav Galic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Madam Registrar. Is the Defence ready to continue the examination-in-chief of the --

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Mr. President. But first of all, could Madam Registrar give us the number of exhibits that will follow, because we have copied pages from the dictionary, and we would like to be able to hand them out with the appropriate number.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. I'd rather deal with the -- with the exhibits after the first break. I take it then that perhaps the videotape is ready, Mr. Ierace?

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: No, it's not, Mr. President. We did some work overnight, and we, just following discussions with Madam Registrar, discovered a further need for compilation. We'll have that ready by the end of the first break.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. That's the reason why I would like to wait until then, so that all parties have everything ready we need. Madam Usher, could you please escort the witness into the courtroom.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Good morning, General Radinovic. Please be seated.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I take it that you can still hear me in a language you understand?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: May I remind you that you are still bound by the solemn declaration you've given at the beginning of your testimony yesterday.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I know.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Then, Ms. Pilipovic, please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Good morning to everyone.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Examined by Ms. Pilipovic: [Continued]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning, General.

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN RADINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Good morning.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: General, yesterday we stopped when talking about the position of the Sarajevo Romanija Corps when General Galic was appointed as corps commander. You spoke about two positions which changed during the period that General Galic was at the command post. My question is with regard to the remaining part of the front. What was the front like and what was the situation like when General Galic became head of the corps?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN RADINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I mentioned two changes on the western front, near Otes, and General Galic managed to improve the tactical position on Otes, that's this area here. But he lost this position here at Zuc. General Galic also lost part of the front at the Nisici plateau. That was here. And when he was leaving, he lost this part of the front. That was one of the weakest points in the operative position of the SRK. When General Galic came to the head of the SRK, I would use a certain expression which would be that at the time the corps was in a state of disintegration. It was chaotic. It didn't have a corps commander until General Galic arrived at the beginning of September 1992. At that time three commanders had left the corps. On the 10th of May, General Dzurdzevac was retired. He was replaced by his deputy for logistics, Dragovic, who also left. And General Sipcic, who was appointed as corps commander, he also left his duties and went over to the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia and he did not return. So General Galic came to the post when there was no commander and there was no one who could transfer the duties of commander to him.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: General, I'm going to return to the issue of what General Galic took over when he became corps commander. In your assessment, in your opinion, and on the basis of the documents that you analysed, can you tell us -- you said the dynamics at the front did not change significantly. What did you mean by that?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN RADINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: When I spoke about the dynamics at the front, I meant significant changes on the front, that is to say, taking large areas from one or the other sides in the conflict. So that's why I only pointed out these three major changes. But there were -- there was a greater number of changes in tactical terms. The front would move by 100 metres, for example. There were these small fluctuations which constantly occurred because the front in Sarajevo was always in changing -- there was almost not a single document that does not show that while he was on duty, there was ongoing combat. General Galic, when he assumed his duty, it should be pointed out that that was a period during which an operation of the 1st BH Army Corps was carrying out, and it was called Operation South. This operation was carried out in the direction of Trnovo, Jahorina, Krupac. That's this direction here. And towards Igman the task was to separate the forces of the Sarajevo Corps from Igman, to isolate the Igman Brigade, part of the Ilijas Brigade -- part of the Ilidza Brigade, and to join up with forces who acted from the direction of Visoko, which were grouped within the tactical -- as part of the tactical group Visoko. This operation was led by a special operative command called the Command for the South. That had a status of an operative group. But the main forces carrying it out belonged to Tactical Group 2. There were about 5 or 6 thousand men and they had 25 artillery pieces and five tanks. This force was not -- was quite strong for that time, the middle of August 1992 to 17th of September, 1992. That's the period of that operation. It didn't succeed. The forces of the 1st Corps were not able to join up with the Visoko Tactical Group probably because they obstructed the link between Tactical Group 2 and the Tactical Group Visoko. Probably because of that reason there were HVO forces that were also there.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. General, you spoke about Operation South that had been taken over by the 1st Corps of the BH army, and you told us that in the course of the operation General Galic became the commander. While General Galic was on duty, occupied this post, were there any other operations? We're talking about operations of the BH army on the front in the area of the SRK. And later I'll ask you about the zone of the SRK. First of all, could you tell us whether there were any other operations in the Sarajevo theatre.

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN RADINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, there were. But in the documents they're called operations, but for a certain type of combat operations to be considered as operations significant forces have to be included. They have to be forces of an operative level, several brigades, a corps, an operative group which is fairly strong. So those operations and really not such, and not at that level, but they were tactical operations which were quite ambitious. That was the Koverat and Jahorina operation, the Life or Death Operation. These were the main operations that were carried out by the units of the 1st Corps. And on the side of the Sarajevo Romanija Corps, there were several operations, the operation for Otes. We have already spoken about this. There was the Mac 2 operation, a part of the preparations for Operation Lukavac 93. And the most ambitious operation which was carried out by the SRK, it was the main staff of the Army of Republika Srpska that led this operation, it was Lukavac 93. This was the most important operation. Finished in August 1993, and the code for that operation was Lukavac 93, and this operation finished when in the Geneva negotiations Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. the president of BH, Alija Izetbegovic, threatened to leave the Geneva negotiations if the operation wasn't brought to an end, and under the pressure of the International Community, the Army of Republika Srpska brought that operation to an end and there was an agreement that the army should withdraw to the initial positions before the beginning of the operation.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: General, that is what you said, but very briefly, what was the purpose of the Operation Lukavac 93?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN RADINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The main problem of the SRK in that direction was the fact that the corridor, Sarajevo-Gorazde via Trnovo was under constant threat. That's this direction here.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN RADINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's the Krupac-Trnovo direction.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Which part of the front?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN RADINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's the southern front. It goes from Krupac through Trnovo and continues towards Podrinje and Herzegovina. That direction was used for an operational link between the SRK and the Herzegovina Corps. A link was secured between those two units. And in the geostrategic sense, a link was ensured between Herzegovina, Podrinje, and the Romanija plateau as parts of the area of Republika Srpska, and the army, as the forces that controlled the area in combat -- in a combat sense were not to allow the operative position to be threatened because -- and for there to be no connection. In Operation Lukavac 93, this operation was planned and carried out in order to liberate that route, to ensure that there was a link between the Herzegovina and the Romanija Corps, a territorial link, and in order to control the area between Igman, Bjelasnica, Jahorina, and Treskavica. So that is the area concerned, this area here.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: General, which part of the front are you pointing to?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN RADINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm pointing to a part of the front in the south of Sarajevo. This is Igman. And we have Bjelasnica here. This is Treskavica and this is Jahorina. So that's the area concerned.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: General, now that you have analysed the operations and the operational positions of the SRK and of the 1st Corps, can you tell us, on this map can you see the entire operative positions -- all the operative positions of the SRK?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN RADINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Naturally, whoever is able to read a map can do this. I think even a layman can do this. You don't have to be specially trained to notice this. The SRK had two major problems in the Sarajevo theatre of war, and that was not to allow forces from the urban part of town to penetrate and join up with forces outside the front, the external front. If that had happened, if the SRK had allowed this to happen, then the route would have been cut off from the Nisici plateau through Semizovac, Ilijas, and Vogosca, and Igman would have been connected to the Nisici plateau and then all the forces west of that line would have been surrounded and threatened with destruction. The 1st Corps would have been able to have a great operational basis in this area, and in that case the war in the Sarajevo theatre of war would have come to an end and the Republika Srpska army would have suffered from this. So the positions of the SRK in the Sarajevo theatre had a key role to play in the entire war in the territory of Bosnia and Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. General, when you were speaking about the map, you mentioned the positions of the SRK, as well as the positions of the 1st Corps of the BH army. You told us that while you were preparing your report you visited Sarajevo. General, bearing in mind the claim by the Prosecution that the SRK had the dominant elevations in the Sarajevo theatre of war, that they were under their control, did your research confirm such a position?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN RADINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, my research didn't confirm such a position. My research confirmed that the 1st Corps of the BH army, with regard to the elevations around Sarajevo, they had an advantage in terms of the elevations occupied around Sarajevo. I'd just like to point out to these features on the map. And while preparing my report and when I visited Sarajevo for research purposes, I photographed these features, and if necessary this could be seen. I don't know if this will be feasible, if this will be possible, but I'll try to explain this to you by using the map. When you have a look at the external front, the elevated features, the features of greatest quality, that would be the Igman feature. That would be the most elevated feature.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: For the sake of the transcript, that's the western part of the front.

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN RADINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The south-western part of the front. That's Igman and Ormanj. That is to the west of Hadzici. Igman is an elevated feature. It enables you to control the entire Sarajevo area from -- to Krupac, Vojkovici, Gornji Kotorac, all the way to Vraca. And you can also control the entire airport part, the Butmir part, Nedzarici, Ilidza, Vrelo Bosne, the entire area to the west -- or rather, to the north and north-east of Igman. Throughout the wartime period, the BH army 1st Corps were on Igman and Ormanj. As far as elevated features are concerned, around the outer ring of Sarajevo you can notice Trebevici. On the slopes of Trebevici, the northern slopes, the SRK forces were present there, and they controlled the eastern part of the town from those positions. So that is to say, from Grbavica to Kneginjac, that is to say, the settlements of Bistrik to the extreme eastern part of Sarajevo. As far as Trebevici is concerned as a position of the 1st Corps, in front of Trebevici and -- there's a chain of features which are very interesting for the army positions. That's Velika Colina Kapa, Mala Colina Kapa, and Debelo Brdo. At these positions you had the first -- the forces of the 1st Corps of the BH army during the main period of the war, and you can see that the elevated position in the direction of Sarajevo from Trebevici was under threat by these suburban positions between the town and Trebevici, to the north of Sarajevo. I'm pointing to the Grdonj Hill and units of the 1st BH Corps were there, and from that position the entire area of Sedrenik can be controlled and the settlements towards the central part of the town and to the west towards Kosevo. I'm pointing to the Hum Hill. Throughout the war, Hum was in the hands of the 1st BH army Corps and from Hum it was possible to control Velesici, Pofalici, that entire area of Bjelava, Groblje [phoen], Bare around Kosevo, and then from Hum a chain of elevated features extends toward Orlic, Zuc, Brijesce Brdo, and Sokolje. And all these positions for the war and in Zuc and Brijesce Brdo, the 1st Corps was there from December 1992. From those positions, from Orlici and Zuc, it was possible to fully control Vogosca, that entire area to the north. And to a significant extent, the advantages of the Army of Republika Srpska was negated. That is to say, the 1st Corps which had positions in Mrkovici and Radava. If we had the opportunity to see the panorama photograph, we'll see that the positions of the 1st Corps were just above Vogosca. Vogosca was more or less at your feet. There's a sign for a minefield there. And from Zuc and Brijesce Brdo, it was possible to control Rajlovac and the entire valley towards Ilidza. And for the town in particular, I'm pointing to the Mojmilo Hill, it's about 2, 2 and a half kilometres. That's the length. And for that entire length, right up to the foot of the hill, you had the positions of the 1st Corps of the BH army. And from that position, from those features, from Mojmilo, you could control Grbavica, Lukavica, Dobrinja, Nedzarici, and Ilidza. So my research and my decisive conclusion was that it's very hard to accept the claim that the SRK, as far as the elevations are concerned, that they had any kind of advantage. In fact, they were disadvantaged. That's my conviction and my knowledge.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you, General. The Defence's plan was to show the video now, but because our time is restricted now, the Defence will show the videotape at the end of your examination-in-chief. My question would now be, following what you told us about combat and battles and about the operations and tactical positions of both armies: Can you tell us first, in your opinion what was -- which side preferred the front to be quiet?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Mr. Mundis. Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Mr. President, the Prosecution would object to that question, but prior to addressing that issue, again there have been numerous references to the map. And I'm wondering if Ms. Pilipovic was intending on indicating what the witness has pointed to for the record.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. But the witness usually mentioned the names of the elevations which have been mentioned so many times that the Chamber considers that we're talk about Zuc or about Mojmilo or about Debelo Brdo that it is sufficiently known to the Chamber what the witness is referring to.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: With respect to the objection to the question, Mr. President, it's an invitation to speculate with respect to which side preferred the front to be quiet.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Ms. Pilipovic, is it a matter of military expertise, or is it a matter of appreciation of facts that you're asking about?

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, this is a question of military expertise. And bearing in mind the documents and considering everything that the general used as an expert, we think that he could answer such a question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Then at least you should be specific as to the sources, because as you know, the transparency of the expert's opinions in relation of facts and methodology used is of great importance for the Chamber. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: General, you told us which documents you used to your expertise. These documents, do they belong to both warring sides?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN RADINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You said that you studied many documents. Is it on the basis of those documents that you've studied and on the basis that you used for the research to make your report, can you tell us, would you be able to draw conclusion which warring side preferred the front to be quiet?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN RADINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, before I answer directly --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: When you answer that question, would you please refer to the specific sources on which you rely when giving your opinion on that. Ms. Pilipovic, you referred very much in general to the documents, which does not then able the Chamber to follow exactly the reasoning of the expert. So would you please then refer to -- on the basis of this document, that document, you find this here, you find that there, so that we can follow exactly what underlies your opinion. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, I studied the documents of both sides, documents from negotiations, requests that sides submitted to the United Nations, to UNPROFOR. Further, I read several studies written by direct participants in the events. These were members of international forces. I mean, first of all, General Rose, who was the commander of UNPROFOR for BH. And I also read the reports made by observers and monitors of the United Nations, and I also have some personal knowledge and personal experience. I was a credited military expert in the delegation of the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia in Geneva negotiations for five months, so I'm very well aware of what Federal Republic of Yugoslavia delegation wanted and what the Republika Srpska delegation wanted, considering that the strategic objective that was placed under Sarajevo was already --

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Mr. President, the Prosecution would have an objection, and we'd like to address that in the absence of the witness, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Then I have to ask you, General Radinovic, to follow the usher and leave the room just for a second so that we can deal with the -- deal with the procedural matter.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I will leave, but I think it will be more natural for me to finish my answer and then to be excluded.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: [Previous interpretation continues] ... What is the most logical way, this is a legal procedural matter, and the Chamber will first hear the parties. So would you please follow the usher.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Mundis.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Mr. President, the Prosecution's position with respect to transparency is clear to the Chamber. Let me just address a couple of issues that form the basis of our objection with respect to what the witness has just said. He's indicated, again without specifying, a large number of documents that he reviewed. He told us yesterday that he's looked at more than ten -- I think his quote was tens of thousands of pages. That's one concern in light of the directions the Chamber just gave to the Defence and to the witness. We're also concerned, Mr. President, about the possibility that this witness will be talking as a fact witness based on his accreditation to certain negotiations wherein he represented the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia at those negotiations and the fact that that's not fully addressed in his report and also the fact that it may appear as though in responding to this question this witness might be crossing into the threshold of being a fact witness rather than an expert witness. And I'm not sure if this problem will arise in the future, but the Prosecution would object to this expert witness testifying as to -- or being in the position of testifying as a factual witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Ms. Pilipovic.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Just a moment, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, bearing in mind the objection of my learned colleague, we would like to point out that General Radinovic has been admittedly an expert for many years, and precisely considering all of the functions that he had throughout the relevant period, we believe that this comes within the area of his expertise, that he should be able to answer such questions. But also bearing in mind the time that has been allocated to the Defence and the intention of the Defence to tender so many exhibits through this witness, the Defence would like to withdraw this question and proceed further. I just wish to say that the expert did say that he was a member of the delegation precisely because he was in a position to find out personally about the issues in question. But as I'm saying, I will withdraw this question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. If you are referring to specific knowledge of the witness - for example, because he has been present during the negotiations or whatever he was - then I think it would be wise then to make a clear distinction in the way you question him, whether you are his -- asking his expertise as an opinion or whether you are seeking information he has obtained during these negotiations, apart from, of course, the matter on whether it's clear from the report and that the Prosecution could expect such a thing. But it's always wise to have a clear distinction between where he talks about facts observed by himself and where he draws conclusions from information which he specified in the report. And I think it could not come as a surprise that where the Prosecution says that it's sometimes unclear what the factual basis is, that this matter has been dealt with before and the Chamber has given its opinion. Of course the report now and then gives facts without precise sources of the basis on which they were established. But I think it's important for the Defence to make a clear distinction between opinion and fact, and if there's a fact, to establish what is the basis of -- on which the witness could testify about these facts. Then please escort the witness into the courtroom again, Madam Usher.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: You may proceed, Ms. Pilipovic. Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: General, can we just please have an answer you started to answer. You personally, what do you know as a participant of the negotiations between the warring sides in Geneva, so your personal knowledge about which side preferred? Were you able to obtain such information and to find out which side preferred for the front to be quiet?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN RADINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I was just interrupted as I was about to give that part of the answer. I know personally that the delegation of Republika Srpska from 1992 asked and insisted on stopping the war in Sarajevo and to begin a political process and seek for a political solution. Why this didn't happen, it's a very long and sad story, and I am not answering that question, but I came across many protests and requests by General Galic asking, immediately after he came to the post of the commander, to uphold the cease-fire that was in force then. I believe that there was a document dated 28th of November, I believe, when General Galic is asking through the UNPROFOR for the cease-fire to be respected because that was a chance to start establishing peace, because if the -- if there was -- if the hostilities continued and if the 1st Corps continued to fight its forces, then there would be very little chance for peace. I believe this was very convincing for me that he was asking for the front to remain calm, to stay calm. And now, on the basis of the analysis of the main objectives which is very hard to call on a specific document, one of the objectives of Republika Srpska was the division of Sarajevo and its Muslim and its Serb side. And when General Galic came to the post, this was already established and there was no need for the hostilities to continue.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: General, we will come back to that. Now I'd like to have an answer from you. In your report you also dealt with and you explained a great deal about the kind of weapons that both warring sides had at their disposal. Could you tell us briefly, in terms of weaponry of the 1st Corps and the SRK.

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN RADINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I would start with the easier part of that. The SRK had good weapons, and the Sarajevo Romanija Corps had an advantage in the terms of high calibre weapons and they were of better quality pieces. And I mean particularly the higher calibre weapons. So throughout my testimony here, so that we don't have to repeat this, I think there's no need to stress this fact. SRK had an advantage in heavier weapons, and it had a definite advantage. However, this advantage did melt as the war progressed, and we can say that already in 1993 the 1st Corps of BH army also had at their disposal a very good arsenal of weapons for giving fire support.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: General, can you tell us which heavy weapons, based on your research, did the 1st Corps of BH army have at their disposal?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN RADINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The 1st Corps had all kinds of heavy weapons and that the SRK had as well, but they didn't have as many pieces. So they had mortars of all calibres and they had field guns, including 130-millimetre field gun on Igman, and they managed to even fire on Pale. They also had Howitzer 105, 155, 122 millimetres. They had also self-propelled weapons.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: General, we'd like to show you some documents, and that perhaps it is in connection to your answer that you could give us some comment on these documents. These are documents of the BH army. That's D47, 1853, and 243.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: I don't have a translation.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: 247, 1853, 243 -- 224, 1853, and 243. General, while we're waiting for the documents, perhaps you could answer a question in relation to the documents. I wanted to ask you -- yesterday about the area of responsibility. Could you tell us what was the area of responsibility of the Sarajevo Romanija Corps, how wide was it, and what was the commander of the corps responsible in the area of responsibility?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN RADINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The area of responsibility of the SRK was about 2.000 square kilometres according to my calculations. That is far above the norms that were in force then, in terms of the rules of the JNA, and these rules were also adopted by the Army of Republika Srpska. What was even harder was that the front that the corps controlled, this front, at the time when General Galic came to the authority, it was -- the front line was over 400 kilometres, and you can see according to the map that they controlled the front from Zvornik all the way to Gorazde, so the entire Drina River Valley. So when the Drina Corps was established, this part was taken over by the Drina Corps and the SRK remained on the front that as we can see on the map. And this was 237 kilometres long. That was the length of the front line, except that the front line on the outer part was about 182 to 185, while the internal front line was 55 kilometres. So that was the length of the front line. That was also above the standards established. And if we look at that the strength of the corps was far below the standards that are valued for developed army forces, that would be about 250.000, so we can see that such a huge front had to be controlled but -- so few forces, then we can see that the main operative problem of General Galic was that with so few troops keep such a long front where there were not too many troops. It would be very easy to break through it.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you very much, General. Can you tell us, what was the commander responsible for in his area of responsibility?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN RADINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The commander in charge of his area of responsibility, he is in charge of the preparation and conduct of combat operations, what is -- that is the military side of the problem. However, there were many other activities that the corps commander was also in charge of but that he was not responsible for.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When you say there were other things that --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could please the counsel and the witness slow down.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: May I ask you to slow down, because the interpreters have difficulties in translating all your words. And perhaps you could make a short break between question and answer. And if you'd do the same, Ms. Pilipovic.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I will try.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So you said that there was political authority, control of the territory, security --

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN RADINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Support resolving all social problems, water supply, electricity supply, the infrastructure. So there would be a large number of activities that were very important for life but that were not part of the responsibilities of the corps commander. The corps commander was in charge of the military activities.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: General, you can see the document 224 in front of you. I would also ask for document 1853 and 243. Can we also have the 224.

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN RADINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Document 224, that is the document of the 1st Corps, where the corps is analysing combat readiness of his own forces. But what's important to notice here in the part that -- when they're speaking about the enemy side, that is, about the Sarajevo Romanija Corps, they say the Sarajevo Romanija Corps is surrounded by seven brigades by about 8.000 troops. That is a very indicative fact for the combat readiness of that corps. There would be 8.000 compared to 55.000 that were in the city, that is, not such a strength that would ensure the positions being kept.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: General, from this document, I would like to show you on the other side 573 in B/C/S. If you can give us your observation, considering this is an estimation of combat readiness of the 1st Corps. According to the --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could the counsel slow down when reading.

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN RADINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm sorry, I can't find this.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: This is the second page of this document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could you slow down when you are reading.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So this is the second page at the end. "There is -- there are no safe data that the enemy has. One line at the end -- no, at the front, at the front of the defence and in terms of depth, it doesn't have fortified lines."

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN RADINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, this speaks about the combat disposition of the Sarajevo Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. Romanija Corps units on the Sarajevo front. So that means that the commander of the 1st Corps assessed that the depth of the defence of the 1st Corps is very short and that means that it only had one line and the depth had nothing.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I think you're talking about the 1st Corps.

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN RADINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. He is assessing his own forces and he is assessing the enemy forces, and he is saying that this is not very strong. I'm apologising. So the 1st Corps Commander is assessing the combat readiness of his own opponent and he's saying that the Sarajevo Romanija Corps, that they have only one line without any depth, without any reserves.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: General, in the documents that you studied for your report, did you get to any facts or data as to what was the front line of the BH army?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN RADINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I came across documents where those who make assessments but do not belong to the corps, that is, the observers and some of the UNPROFOR members, they always said that the 1st Corps had no depth. Even one observer of the United Nations - I can't remember quite his name - but he said that the 1st Corps didn't even have battalions or companies because he says they didn't need any. But operative documents of the 1st Corps do contain data from which we can see that the corps did have organised defence in three lines, that is, the first line, the reserve, and the units that were preparation -- in preparation and resting for the coming operations.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. General, you can see before you document 1853.

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN RADINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you tell us, that is an SRK document. This is an order by General Stanislav Galic, 16 December 1993. Can you tell us about item 1 of this document.

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN RADINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Item 1 of this document speaks about the situation on the front and a little lower down --

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I mean this item.

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN RADINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It speaks about the 1st Corps. This one, just like the other commander, his opponent, is assessing the situation of his opponent, of the 1st Corps of the BHA. He's analysing and ascertaining which forces he is facing on the other side of the Sarajevo theatre. And he then says these are the 1st, the 2nd, the 5th, the 9th, the 15th, the 101st and 102nd Motorised Brigade, the 1st, 2nd, and 10th Mountain Brigade, the 1st Mixed Artillery Brigade, the Reconnaissance Sabotage Brigade, the HVO Brigade Kralj Tvrtko, Croatian Defence Council, the anti-aircraft defence regiment. The 1st and the 2nd Independent Battalion. The Delta Detachment, al Fatah detachment, special MUP detachment called Lasta, special detachment called Biseri. Special unit Vikic's men, as well as other units, instruction centres, and many other units supporting, the staff and logistic units. He further gives the strength, the disposition, and everything else that fits into everything I have already said in the beginning when I spoke about the general relationship of the forces in the front.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: General, have a look at document 243. It's an addition to the command of the command of the 1st Corps, and it is dated 8th of December, 1993.

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN RADINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Let me just have a look at it, please. Yes. It's an addition to the command of the command of the 1st Corps dated the 8th of December, 1993. It's a standard type. Item 1: "Aggressor." That's how they called the Army of Republika Srpska in the Sarajevo theatre of war. At the bottom of that item there is a paragraph that says, "The battalion," and they are referring to the battalion defending that position in Nedzarici. That was the most difficult operative location in the Sarajevo theatre. "The battalion is mostly brought up to strength with local people. It's composed of local people and refugees from the Zenica region and is not at full establishment strength. And in combat to date, it has had considerable casualties." And this was something characteristic of Nedzarici and throughout the entire wartime period. Some of its companies in one month, they would lose all their men. One company lost 92 men in one month, and that is almost the entire company.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: General, could you have a look at page 2 of the document of the 1st Corps. That's 541 in the Serbian version, item 5.2, given that this is an addition to the command, can you tell us what the command of the 1st Corps, who has provided this addition, states what he has planned under this item.

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN RADINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The form is again standard. The positions expressed aren't appropriate to the doctrine and theory of war. But the type is standard. It gives a task to a company to pass into attack with the 5th Motorised Brigade with one unit in reserve and also to introduce reserves and in cooperation with neighbours to carry on with an attack and clear up the Nedzarici settlement, next to the Aleja Bujica Street [phoen]. So they had to clear the terrain, clear Nedzarici. That means to clear the area of everything that they come across.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. General --

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN RADINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I apologise. Perhaps under item 4 there is also something that is very characteristic of the way the 1st Corps waged war. The commander decided to say that creating panic among Chetniks and civilians, they should launch an attack and group their forces. So the purpose is expressed that civilians should be targeted.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: General, we'll return to that later when my colleague continues questioning you about this document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: May I just interfere. Just for my clarification, when you asked about documents when one party assesses the strength of the other party, was it your purpose to establish what was in the mind of one party in respect of the strength of the other party, or did you intend to establish what the strength actually was?

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, we wanted to establish what the strength of both sides was.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. May I then have one methodological question -- then I have one methodological question. If you want to establish the strength of a force, would you primarily seek the basis for that in what was the assessment of the other party, or would you primarily look at the documents of that warring faction itself in order to see what they knew about their own strength rather than rely upon the assessment which might be a wrong assessment, it might be a right assessment, but there is a risk that the assessment is not correct, whereas the own documentation could be expected to be more precise, more reliable? Could you tell us why you rely upon assessments of the other party rather than on own documents?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, I relied on documents of the side itself, on our own side, and on the side -- on the other side that is involved in the process of gathering information on the opposing side. So the information found in intelligence studies, this is not totally irrelevant, information that we find about the enemy side, these sides in contact on a daily basis, and they know each other fairly well. And my analysis of both sides has proved that there were no significant differences between what the sides claimed about themselves and what one side would claim about the other side.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: So you say since you checked the assessments, they were correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] On the whole these assessments are correct, assessments that are about the units on opposing sides.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Also the strength of units, I mean, the number of -- because we have been confronted with strength also expressed in numbers. I mean, if you say there are ten units and that assessment is correct but there could also be a situation where you say there were ten units comprising 50.000 people where the ten units are correct but the 50.000 is not correct. Is it correct not only in terms of number of units or number of brigades, number of battalions, but is it also correct in respect of the number of men involved? For example, if you say there is an assessment of seven brigades, 8.000 people, would they be both correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] For this corps, yes, that would be Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. correct. As far as the assessments made by the SRK for the 1st Corps, as far as the number of units and the composition and the name of the unit, that's correct. As far as the number, whether it was 4.200, et cetera, that was not important for my analysis and I didn't check that piece of information because no one can be certain that on that day there were -- there was a certain number of men present.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: So you said -- you say now that the assessment to some extent you did not check it, as far as the number of men involved are concerned. I'm asking you this because you earlier mentioned the number of those belonging to the other forces. You compared the number of your people and the number in the other force. But you say when an assessment is used as to the strength of the other party, the number of units, you checked that. But whether the number of men is correct, you didn't check that.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, I didn't check that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: That brings me back to my initial question: Is -- whether from a methodological point of view it would not be better if you are establishing - and because, Ms. Pilipovic, that's what you intended to do - when you are establishing the strength of a force, whether it would not be better to rely upon their own information rather than rely on the assessment of the other party. I'm just asking methodologically whether that would be to be preferred.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That would be preferable, but the parties, when they compile operative documents, they don't mention the strength of the units. They mention the composition of the unit and the task but not the strength, and they don't even mention the composition of the unit with precision. This is for internal use. But when we don't have direct information, then you have to obtain indirect information. And one of the indirect methods is to take into account an assessment that you get from the opposing side. That is a method that is used in military research in general.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Also after the war, because you said this is for internal use, but perhaps after a war you might have access to sources that give this internal information.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, yes, I did that after the war. General Ajnadzic, who was the chief of the staff of the SRK, or rather, of the 1st Corps of the BH army, wrote a book. That was his MA study, and he mentioned the strength of his corps, the strength of the forces at the outside front and the internal front, including the armed police, and that was --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] 78.000 [Realtime transcript read in error "58.000"] men.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: General, you mentioned operative positions and tactical positions of the warring sides. I apologise. It says "58.000" in the transcript. It should say "78.000." Yes, yes. My colleague pointed it out to me. So you said 78.000?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN RADINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, 78.000. That's what Ajnadzic said. I took it from him.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In your report, you also mentioned weapons and you mentioned the weapons that the SRK had. You expressed your opinion. You made an assessment. I would now like to show you documents 247, 1852, 204, and 290.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Would that be 1851 -- 247, 1851?

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] 204 -- yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: General, the four documents that you have in front of you, the first one is dated the 17th of January, 1993. It's from the command of the Igman Brigade. The second is 23/12/92. That's 1851. It's a report from the SRK. 204 is a document of the violations of the cease-fire -- signed by the cease-fire from the command of the SRK. 17/12/1993, that's the date. And document 290, command of the operative group Igman, dated 12 March 1993. General, can you tell us, with regard to these four documents -- these five documents, can you tell us what they are about and what information we can find in them? I'll return to the document on the truce later on.

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN RADINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In document 297 -- 247, 247, it's a report from the command of the Igman Brigade dated the 17th of January, 1993 in which it informs the command of the SRK that on that day, the 17th of January, 1993, this day that Howitzers were used against the civilian population in Hadzici, 105-millimetre Howitzers and 120-millimetre mortars.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. General, the document 23 December, 1851, it's a regular combat report from the Sarajevo Romanija Corps.

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN RADINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. It's dated the 23rd of December, 1992, and the command of the Sarajevo Romanija Corps informs the main staff of the Army of Republika Srpska that the enemy continued strong assault actions on the north-western part of the front and that the enemy artillery, the artillery of the 1st Corps - and this is in relation to the SRK - fired 110 grenades at the Hadzici area. They fired 60 grenades at the Ilidza area, 50 shells at the Rajlovac area, Vogosca and Semizovac were fired at with 120 shells, and 70 shells were fired at the Ilijas area.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. General, document 204 is a document from the Sarajevo Romanija Corps. The date is the 7th of December, 1993. And it is about the violation of the signed truce by the Muslims. Is that the document you have?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN RADINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. That is a document that the command of the SRK used to report to the president of the RS assembly, presumably as a signatory to that truce. They informed that in the period from the 1st of August, 1993, until the 5th of November, 1993, while that truce was in force, the artillery of the 1st Corps fired at Grbavica and Vraca. They fired 101 projectiles at Grbavica and Vraca. They fired 94 projectiles at Dobrinja and Lukavica. And the positions of the 2nd Sarajevo Brigade. That's the area. They fired 44 projectiles at the Vojkovici area and 250 projectiles on the Rajlovac area. At the time of the truce, they fired a total of 1.426 projectiles.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: General, have a look at document 290. It's the command of the operative group Igman.

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN RADINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Let me just have a look. Yes, I remember the document. There was a misunderstanding with regard to obtaining weapons. Certain ammunition was obtained for 152-millimetre Howitzers, and it was forwarded to its destination in the unit and the commander of the 1st Corps was informed that the ammunition was not appropriate for that type of weapon because the operative group Igman has 152-millimetre Howitzers M-84 Nora and Howitzer 152 T-20 Howitzers and the shells can't be used without being modified.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you, General. The documents that you have now analysed for us, do they mention the fact that the 1st Corps of the BH army had heavy weaponry?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN RADINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I showed you the document about the violation of the truce that was signed, and you mentioned this in your report too. Were you able to assess how often truces were signed and on the basis of the documents were you able to assess how frequently these truces were violated and by whom and how long were they in force?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN RADINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: At the moment I don't know how many truces were signed, but there were a lot of them. They were frequently negotiated, probably under the pressure of the International Community. But likewise, those truces were violated even more frequently. So not a single truce was respected. I came across many documents in which the commanders of the SRK complained about violations of truces by the Muslims.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could document 275, 298, and 1849, could these documents be shown to the general.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: General, do you have document 275 from the command of the 102nd Motorised Brigade in front of you?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN RADINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Given that this is an order for using artillery in defence, can you briefly tell us - and items 2, 3, and 4 - what does this document talk about?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN RADINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The command of the 102nd Motorised Brigade - and let me just tell you where that brigade was located - that's this area here, Stup. From Alipasino Bridge to Nedzarici, that's the position that it held. The command of the 102nd Brigade ordered that artillery should be used and requested that the 102nd Motorised Brigade should organise a decisive defence in the Centrotrans zone, the house of pensioners, and Zora factory Sipad. So these are positions on Stup. The brigade artillery group had its positions in Vitkovici, and Vitkovici is here. You can see it here. And it's important to say that in Vitkovici Hill, there were 120-millimetre mortars and there were likewise 120-millimetre mortars on Zestika and 122-millimetre mortars are used and there were also 122-millimetre Howitzers in the Zrak area. This group of 102nd Motorised Brigade had Zis, 60-millimetres mortars, 120-millimetres, rockets, 107 millimetres -- rocket launcher, 107 millimetres. It also had cannons, 76 millimetres. So not a single type of weapon that a brigade of that level would not have.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you, General. You have in front of you the document numbered 298. That's the command of the 1st Corps, dated the 16th of February, 1993. It's an order from the staff of the Supreme Command. Can you tell us, what is being ordered in this order? Briefly.

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN RADINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Document 298 is an order from the command of the 1st Corps of the BH army dated the 16th of February, 1993. And it is an order to disband an artillery brigade and that its organisational units should be disposed -- should be positioned in other war units. First of all, a mortar battery, 120-millimetre battery with all the personnel and the materiel and technical means should be placed within a 3rd Motorised Brigade, and a 3rd Motorised Brigade was located at positions in the direction of Zuc. I apologise, the 3rd Motorised Brigade -- yes. That's where the 3rd Motorised Brigade was located. The 122-millimetre Howitzer battery with the entire crew, and then something is handwritten, should be placed in the 1st Motorised Brigade. I apologise. It's important to say that here you have four battalions, and -- artillery battalions, and it's said that these units should be disbanded and these battalions should be assigned to brigades and that would increase the strength, the firing power, of the brigades.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: General, before the break, have a look at document 1849, which is a command, an order, from the 1st Motorised Brigade. Could you have a look at page 2 of the document 3 -- 2, under item 4, where it says "Decision," the penultimate paragraph under item 4. It says, "The combat disposition with the line." Is that the document?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN RADINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. That's the document I was thinking of when I spoke about the combat disposition of the brigades of the 1st Corps, and here you can clearly see that the combat disposition of that brigade was in two lines with reserves, so up to three lines, in fact, three positions. You can see that that brigade had a depth. It wasn't a classical linear disposition.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. General, on page 3 of this document, item 13, where it says "morale," the last paragraph, it says, and I'll read this out - and then perhaps you could tell us what your position is - it's an order from the 1st Motorised Brigade. "Since the occupation of such a fortified settlement is impossible without destroying and setting fire to objects, which at the same time very strong fortifications, demolish and set fire to everything so that this operation can be carried out safely. Because of the well-known brazenness and lack of principle, don't believe any person, any captured persons, especially those under arms." Can you tell us what the commander of the 1st Motorised Brigade had in mind when he wrote this?

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Objection. Calls for speculation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Of course you could ask the witness how he understands this, what the meaning of it would be, but we cannot ask him what someone had in his mind.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Your Honour. Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So the meaning of the paragraph that I've read out to you, in your opinion.

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN RADINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As far as I can see - and I've had this document in front of me already - this is a document in which the commander of the brigade orders an attack to be carried out against Grbavica. Grbavica is a part of Sarajevo that was under the control of the Army of Republika Srpska, that is to say, under the control of the SRK. In this paragraph the commander is ordering action to be intense, and he's mentioning the attitude towards civilian features. He's ordering that civilian objects should be demolished.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, given that it's time for a break -- Your Honour, could I ask a question. It's of a technical nature. How much time does the Defence have?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: The decision initially was three hours. Then it was four hours. And I think we left an opening that it might be five hours, depending on the way you conduct the examination-in-chief. In this respect, I would like to say that going into many details might not always assist this Chamber, and so therefore I very much would like to stress that the Defence makes clear priorities what are the main issues. But that is how much time you would have, and you used until now approximately two hours and 15 minutes. We'll adjourn until 11.00.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] May I take the floor, please, before the witness comes in. I only need 15 seconds to say the following: We have a technical problem which is very important. One of the maps - and General Galic has now just told me - is that we'd like to show to the expert, and unfortunately this map is -- remained in Geneva. One is in Geneva and one is here. We only have one copy of the map. It's a technical problem which may arise. So this could imply that we will need more time. That's the only thing that we are saying. We're trying to find a solution, but we just want you know now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: May I take it that you do not need more time but you need time at another moment.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I didn't say that I didn't need more time, but if you're inviting me to say that, I'll say it gladly. I wasn't speaking of the time to do with the map, but I can speak about time with pleasure. Very well.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: No. I was just referring to that more time can mean more things. The first is that you need more time in order to finish your preparation or that you need more time for the examination of the witness. I was referring to the first rather than to the second.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, we are practically ready, but we have to specify that we will have to see whether we will need more time later on.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Mundis.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Two items, Mr. President: First, it's unclear to the Prosecution exactly what this map or maps that Mr. Piletta-Zanin is referring to indicate. He indicates that one is in Geneva and one is here. I'm not sure if this is a map that's been disclosed to the Prosecution or not.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I take it -- could the parties please discuss that during the next break so that we'll see whether there's any remaining problem in respect of a map. I think we've got two at this moment. Whether we have three finally or not.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: If I may raise one other issue, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: During the break, we were handed another bundle of documents, apparently which the Defence is intending on putting to the witness. I note from the exhibit numbers those documents which were attached to the Radinovic report bear numbers roughly from D172 to D301, I believe. There are numerous documents on the list I was just handed, and in this bundle that are D1800-series for lack of a better word. There appear to be about ten of them. It does not appear that these were on the exhibit list with respect to this witness. We're make some inquiries and checking these documents now, but it's unclear whether those documents were also in any of the letters which we received from the Defence indicating additional documents they would put to the witness. I've checked a few of them very quickly, and they do not appear to be, Mr. President. So I'm simply raising this now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. You reserve the right to oppose against showing these documents to the witness. I noticed that we had some documents in the 1800-series until now as well. So the Defence can expect that if there would be any - I don't know whether there is - but if there would be any document that was not indicated before, they can expect opposition from the Prosecution. Then I'd like to make two observations, as far as the Chamber is concerned. The Chamber discussed briefly the way the examination-in-chief develops. Looking at it, how it does develop until now, this would not encourage the Chamber to grant five hours instead of four. The second observation is that if the Defence would leave details and come to what the Chamber considers to be points more in --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: There seems to be problem with the transcript. Yes. We -- there are a few lines missing. The second observation, let me start with that, is that the Chamber would -- no, again the transcript seems to be -- whether it's a technical transcription problem. There again seems to be a technical difficulty.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I'm informed that for technical reasons we have to restart and that takes us five minutes to have everything set again to restart. So we'll adjourn for five minutes. --- Break taken at 11.13 a.m.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: The technical problems being solved, we'll restart. I'll just repeat that I said before that until now the way that the examination-in-chief develops does not encourage the Chamber to grant more than the four hours indicated. The second issue is that the Chamber can imagine that in prioritising, there are issues that are of greater relevance than a lot of the details we have dealt with until now and of which we find quite a lot in the report itself, and it may be clear to the parties that the expert testimony is not there to repeat what the report already says. Please proceed. If the witness is brought into the courtroom.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, since we are speaking precisely about methodology and so that we can be clearly in a position to proceed, we don't know whether the witness handed you his homework, as you wished for him to do so.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: No, it has not yet been done.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. Could we perhaps ask him to do this so that we can be certain and save time that we find so precious.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: What homework did you have exactly in mind, Mr. Piletta-Zanin?

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] What you asked him to do, Mr. President, what you asked him yesterday. There were modifications that the witness wanted to put into his text, and you asked him to do that in writing, and I don't think that he has done that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: May I ask you, General, did you already prepare in writing the corrections you'd like to make in respect of your report, as I invited you to do yesterday?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, I have done that, Mr. President. But unfortunately, I don't work on the computer, and I have that written in hand. Perhaps I can dictate it to someone.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Or -- I don't know how your handwriting is. I hope it's better than mine, but --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Not very good. Unfortunately, no, it's poor.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Then perhaps we should provide you with a dictating -- a small machine so you can dictate it and that it will then be worked out.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Do you have such a machine, or do you need one from us?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, I don't have it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. I will personally take care that one is available for you. Then please proceed, Ms. Pilipovic.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: General, in your report, you compiled it and you came to a conclusion that in the Sarajevo theatre there was light infantry weapons that was used; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN RADINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In your research, did you come across documents that you studied and that there was talk that there were snipers used in the Sarajevo theatre?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN RADINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In your research, did you come across data whether the parties had snipers and which side had snipers, if they did have snipers?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN RADINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In my research, I managed to establish that the SRK during the mandate of General Galic had snipers 7.9 millimetres, semi-automatic rifle, and snipers of calibre 7.62 millimetres, while the 1st Corps of the BH army had those very same snipers, as well as 12.7-millimetre snipers.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you tell us a little more precisely. When you say that SRK had snipers, can you explain that.

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN RADINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: SRK, according to its establishment in the units of the brigades, would have one sniper per section, except that I have to say that I checked this data in talking to the brigade commanders. When I spoke to the commander of the Kosevo Brigade, Mr. Krajisnik - I think that's his name, Krajisnik - he told me that to start with, until 1993, mid-1993, had no snipers at all. The same thing I heard from General Istej [phoen], commander of the 1st Romanija Brigade, who said that not in all of the battalions in their sections there were snipers.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. When we're talking about your research into BH army, what data did you obtain --

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, the Defence would like to show the general documents 279, 1855, 281, 242.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed. Yes, Mr. Mundis.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Mr. President, while that's being done, the Prosecution would reiterate its request for the notes of the expert with respect to the two individuals that he just spoke of and that was the basis of his testimony.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Did you make any notes of the interviews you had, for example, with Mr. Krajisnik?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [No audible response]

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. You have these notes?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Would you provide them to us.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Did you provide them to the counsel before?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Unfortunately, when I gave the whole bundle of conversations, unfortunately the interview notes from Krajisnik and Ugresic conversations fell out, but I have them on me. Do you want me to hand it over now or during the break?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Perhaps we'll wait until ... So I do understand that you provided your notes in the past to Defence counsel, apart from the Krajisnik and the Ugresic notes; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: May I also ask you: Did you have any hesitation to give these notes on whatever basis to this court?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: It was not on the basis of confidentiality that you felt that you could not give these notes to anyone?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, not at all. It's a working -- it was a working paper.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] While I was preparing for my report, and I spoke to people that I believed could give me important information. So this is just a free-style notes. It's not a standardised questionnaire. Of course I have no problem in handed that over.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: You did not promise those persons that you would keep confidential what the conversation was about?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] They didn't ask me, and I didn't say anything.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Please proceed, Ms. Pilipovic.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Oh, yes -- one moment.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: You may now provide the notes that you had of these conversations with Mr. Krajisnik and Ugresic to Madam Registrar. We'll return the original to you, but they'll be copied so that the parties can look at it. You just said that you had them with you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I can do that immediately?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, please.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: The witness has just been given document 279, 146, 1855, 280, 241, 220, 216, 214, 210.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] If you please.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: General, you have before you documents of the BH army. Can you briefly look at them and tell us if these are the documents that you used and from which you drew your opinion that in the Sarajevo theatre units of the 1st Corps of the BH army had snipers, then they had training, that snipers were operational throughout and what their positions were. Are these those documents? Could you please look at them and tell us, General, bearing in mind the time we have is limited. You don't have to analyse each document individually, but can you just please look at them and tell us if these are these documents.

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN RADINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I have before me order of the commander of the 2nd Motorised Brigade of the 1st Corps of the BH army.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The next document?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN RADINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is the order of the commander of the 1st Motorised Brigade and the order of another commander of a motorised brigade, the 1st Motorised Brigade, and of some army unit without clear identification which unit is in question; it simply says "army unit." In the first document the order says that "all snipers that the brigade has has to be put in permanent constant function 24 hours."

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you, General. The other documents, do they also speak about the same things?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN RADINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, they speak about the same things. But the document from the 2nd of October, 1993, is interesting from the point of view that there is a sniper platoon that is being established. So the 1st Motorised Brigade from its three battalions makes -- or establishes a sniper platoon in the first item.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you, General. The documents that are also marked, you can just call out the numbers of the documents.

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN RADINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In the document D280, there is an order for the snipers to be grouped in the 1st Corps.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you, General. General, the other documents that you used, are they also about this?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN RADINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, they are. I also came across a document that now I can't find, to be honest, here and from which you can see that the 1st Corps also has snipers using 12.7-millimetre gun. It says -- one of the documents says that all snipers should be combat ready, including snipers using 12.7-millimetre calibre gun. That would be a good thing to find this document. It would be a pity not to find it. But this is certainly that should be found. I have quoted all these documents.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. Since this is quoted, cited in the report, then we don't have to find it. So you're telling us these are documents where it says that snipers were operational in the Sarajevo theatre of war.

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN RADINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you, General. General, you told us that General Galic became a commander of the SRK on the 7th of September, 1992. Can you tell us, in your expertise, you wrote a great deal about, this but can you tell us how did that come about that at the time Colonel - at that time - Stanislav Galic came to be the commander of the Sarajevo Romanija Corps, and what was the situation in the battlefield in the combat area that he encountered? And this is to do with the takeover of his duties and the organisation of his system of command and control in the Sarajevo theatre.

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN RADINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: General Galic came to the commander of the SRK from being the commander of the 30th Division, that is, of course, an honour for any officer and General Galic, still as a young officer, when he was recruited to be the -- in the support battalion of the main staff, he was part of the elite of the then-JNA units and certainly before him he had a brilliant career and to be appointed corps commander, that is the crown of such a career. And I also know in this sense that the unit that General Galic commanded in the 5th military district in Ljubljana was supposed to be transferred to Valjevo and certainly this could not have suited him because of the family situation, which was quite unfavourable for him because his children continued to live in Slovenia, so this was a very painful, not to be with his family. His wife was Hungarian, and he thought that it would be completely normal to go to Federal Republic of Yugoslavia to be in Serbia, where Serbian language is spoken, where there would be a new war adventure in Bosnia. He really didn't need that. But a soldier doesn't need -- doesn't ask about his duties and he's not in a position to choose.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. General, with which problems or which problems did he face, General Galic, when he came to be the commander of the corps command?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Mundis.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Objection, Mr. President. This line of questioning seems to follow very closely pages 90 - excuse me - 92 through 94 of the expert's statement, and I note that none of that material is sourced, and we would challenge this evidence unless a proper foundation for the source of this information has been established.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Could you please respond whether this does reflect, these pages, and whether there are any sources available.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
