utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, it is a reflection -- the expert said that he has personal knowledge as well when he answered my question and explained this, and I asked this question to lead up to the question as to what General Galic took over when he was appointed as commander of the SRK and in order to show the witness certain documents.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: General, what did General Galic take over when he was appointed --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: There is an objection. I would first like to look at it in more detail. I note, Ms. Pilipovic, that none of the pages -- that most of the pages mentioned are relatively poor of indication of sources. So therefore, if you'd like to deal with any of these issues, would you please lay the proper foundation.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: General, when you answered the question in the biography of General Galic, when talking about General Galic's background, can you tell us what the sources of the information are.

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN RADINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As assistant to the Minister for Strategy, that was my last duty in the army in the course of -- when the former Yugoslavia was disintegrating and before the units were transferred. At that time I participated in the planning, and I personally know that General Galic's division was to be transferred to Valjevo. Because it was on a route attacked by Croatian paramilitary forces, for that reason the Supreme Command diverted that brigade, that column, to Banja Luka and Galic arrived in Banja Luka instead of arriving in Valjevo. This is something that I know and I am sure it can be checked in other sources, but I have personal knowledge of this. I don't know what kind of documents I could show you in order to convince you of this.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. General, you told us that in the Sarajevo theatre of war when the general was at the time a colonel, when he arrived there and was appointed as commander, at that time three commanders had already left that theatre of war. Can you tell us what the commander -- what duties Colonel Galic took over and what measures did he take for reorganising the command system. What sort of problems confronted him, first of all, and what action did he take?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN RADINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The main problem that Colonel Galic had when he arrived at the command of the SRK was the ongoing action of the 1st Corps. And I have said that it was called Operation South. The Rogoj area was lost in that action, which links Brno with the area towards Foca, the pass, that pass was lost, Trnovo was lost. There were serious crimes committed against the Serbian population.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: General, since you have written about this in detail, could you briefly tell us what other problems General Galic came across.

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN RADINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, stopping the Operation South was the key problem, the most urgent issue. Secondly, it was necessary to stabilise the fronts in other parts of the battlefield. Thirdly, it was necessary to visit the zone of responsibility, to talk to the commanders, to see what the situation was in the field, to organise the system of command because combat reports would not arrive regularly from all the units and from some units they didn't arrive at all. From the Igman Brigade, for example, there weren't any reports for a certain period of time. Other units would not send reports on a regular basis. The operative centre and the operative command wasn't functioning properly. There wasn't an information centre for the corps for public relations. In that zone of responsibility of the SRK there were several very important military and industrial facilities intended for special purposes. They produced weapons and ammunition.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: General, did he come across other concrete problems?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN RADINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: There were political problems, high-level politics, and problems that concerned local politics. There were local politicians who would get directly involved in the system of command. There were problems with paramilitary forces. This was also a very serious problem at the time. In brief, there were a lot of serious problems that Colonel Galic had to confront in a short period of time and had to solve in order to organise a system of command and control, an efficient system of command and control.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, I'd like to show the witness the following documents: 1854, 1857, 1858, 264, and 265.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: General, to these documents, 1854, 16 September 1992 signed by General Galic; 1857, 22/9/92; 1858, the same date, 22 October 1992; 264, 12 October 1994, 265. Do these documents mention what General Galic did when he was appointed as corps commander?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN RADINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. This is a series of documents in which you can see the measures that Galic took in order to organise the system of command in his corps. There's an order saying how reports should be submitted and on what subjects and when. The second document has to do with assigning teams for command. This is a condition for the efficient functioning of the operations centre; that is to say, the command post, and also has to do with what to do when commander is not in the command. Then there is an order from the corps commander which mentions measures for dealing with shortcomings, and this has to do with the organisation in the corps, the order in the corps, and then there are measures that have to do with regulating the circulation of unauthorised persons and have to do with relations with UNPROFOR and the civilian authorities, relations with UNPROFOR, the mission, the liaison section, the liaison team for UNPROFOR. And document 264 is an order from the corps commander which orders that behavious towards civilians should be strictly regulated, civilians who are not Serbian in his zone of responsibility. Item 1, it says --

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: General, it's not necessary for you to read out from these documents. The following document is also a document in which General Galic orders --

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN RADINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. He orders alcohol being provided and says that you should respect competence, the hierarchy when communicating with the superior command, and also when you may address the main staff and there's an entire system of measures which organise the system of command. I haven't seen any documents here. I've had them in my hands, and perhaps it's my fault for not having set them aside, but there are documents where the commander of the SRK orders the system of communication to be used through documents for the secret of command of troops. So it's a system of coded documents and coded communications which is being ordered. And he installed an informations centre for the corps which was to be responsible for communicating with the public. So the entire system of command was being organised in a way that was regulated by the rules.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. General, you told us that in the area you mentioned the weapons of the SRK. Can you tell us what General Galic did, what steps did he take, in order to organise the use of the artillery.

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN RADINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I came across over 25 documents which were orders of Galic's and had to do with regulating the use of the artillery in the Sarajevo theatre of war. In all of those documents which I had at my disposal, he explicitly forbid the use of the artillery if this had not been ordered and if targets had not been identified, and he said that no one had the right to target civilian features and settlements.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. General, the Defence will show you document 238, 193 -- 238, 193, 258, 251, and 257.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Ms. Pilipovic, just for the sake of the transcript, although the Chamber has difficulties in following every detail, but on page 49, line 3, the answer reads: "Yes, he orders alcohol being provided and says that you should respect competence ..." If this was a reference to documents --

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Forbids it, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: [Previous interpretation continues] ... I rather read that "it's most strictly forbidden to deliver and consume alcohol." So I take it that it's a mistake. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: General, do you have the documents in front of you, the documents that say how the use of the artillery is regulated? It's document 238, that the command of the SRK adopted on the 23rd of June, 1992, and it's signed by Commander Tomislav Sipcic?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN RADINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. It forbids the use of all artillery in the corps zone.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: General, document 193, is that also a document about the locations --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Ms. Pilipovic, it was just reference was made to 238, I think. It was said -- you asked -- yes, "it forbids the use of all the artillery in the corps zone." What I read, but perhaps I'm wrong, in 238 is "usage of all artillery weapons in corps zone is prohibited. Only corps commander may permit the usage of artillery weapons." That is two lines, instead of the one line just read. Could I ask you whether I correctly understand this that the --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Could you please use your microphone.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, the entire document has been translated.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. But you're -- the answer of the witness was that this document forbids the use of all artillery in the corps zone.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, I agree.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: When I read that relatively short document, it says that it's forbidden to use any artillery weapons without the consent of the corps commander. Is that a correct understanding of this document?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You've understood that correctly.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] But I wasn't given the opportunity to read it out by the Defence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: General, document 193, does it also mention locations and can you tell us whether this document has anything to do with grouping the artillery dated -- the document is dated the 14th of June, 1992.

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN RADINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. This document follows the agreement on handing the airport over to UNPROFOR, placing the airport under the control of UNPROFOR. The Army of Republika Srpska handed the airport over to UNPROFOR. It was to control it, and it was to be used for humanitarian purposes and for the purposes -- for the needs of the UN. And all the brigades in the vicinity of the airport undertook to group the artillery in certain locations so that they could be controlled, or rather, so that it would be possible to prevent fire from being opened. So this is the first process of strictly controlling the artillery of the SRK that was positioned around Sarajevo.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. General, do the other documents also mention the organisation and use of artillery in the Sarajevo theatre of war?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN RADINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. All of these orders -- I don't know if it's necessary for me to read them out --

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Just tell us whether those orders confirm what you have just said.

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN RADINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Yes, they very explicitly order the establishment of full control over artillery use.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. General, you told us that General Stanislav Galic was confronted with the problem of paramilitary forces and the problem of civilian authorities. The Defence would like to show you document 229, 1860, 197, 198, and 199. General, the documents 229, 1860, 197, 198, and 199, are these documents that show that General Galic did everything that was in his power, so to speak --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Mundis.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Mr. President, the Prosecution doesn't seem to have all of these documents, or at least the documents that we do have that are next in the bundle don't have exhibit numbers on them. So perhaps if somehow my colleague could perhaps provide the dates of those documents, I might be able to fill in the exhibit numbers.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Ms. Pilipovic, we find the same problem, that some of these documents are not numbered, although stamped. Until now, we found them all in the subsequent order, so --

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That's a mistake. I'll give the dates. 8th of August, 1992, that's the date for document 229. The 3rd of November, 1992, combat report, that's document 1860, the command of the Tactical Group of Vogosca. The 27th of August, 1993, report on taking measures with regard to the Vaske [phoen] case, 27th of August, 1993.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: You should then give us the numbers as well. The command of the tactical group of Vogosca -- it goes too quick for me. The 27th of August, 1993, is that number 197?

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Then the next one, 198, is numbered and is also the 27th of August; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Then 199 is numbered. Is yours numbered as well, Mr. Mundis?

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Yes, it is. Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Then we have one which is even without a stamp, it seems, and that is a document also of the 27th of August, 1993, which in the translation it starts with "very urgent." It's number 20/15 and then "982." What number would that have, Ms. Pilipovic?

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Let me just ask my associate. The last number, which number is the last one? 1911.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: General, do these documents mention all the measures taken by General Galic with regard to paramilitary formations, and which measures did he take? And when I say "all the measures," I mean some of the measures that he may have taken and which measures were they?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN RADINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In these documents, it mentions measures General Galic took to solve the crisis with paramilitary formations, the measures he took to prevent paramilitary formations from acting in his zone of responsibility. And document 229 illustrates what Galic's attitude was towards the paramilitary formations, inappropriate behaviour in his zone of behaviour. And you can see that as soon as he assumed the duties of commander of the SRK he took the same measures in order to prevent paramilitary forces to act in his zone of responsibility because this disrupted the system of command.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: General --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I'd just ask, because it goes very quickly at this very moment. The document you referred to that would indicate that he overcame all the problems with the paramilitary formations -- it just says what action he took, not whether he was successful in that. But perhaps you could answer that question, whether the measures that he took to overcome the problems with the paramilitary formations were successful or that there remained some problems.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] While General Galic was in the position he had, he had problems with the paramilitary formations but he solved some of the problems. He replaced the commander of the Igman Brigade, who was at the limits -- whose behaviour was at the limits of paramilitary behaviour. To an extent he managed to solve the question of relations with the authorities, with the organs of power.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. We don't need to go into details. But you said he solved some of the problems. I do understand. Not all, but some of them. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: General, you told us that General Galic also confronted the problem that concerned the civilian authorities.

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN RADINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you tell us whether General Galic in some way managed to solve those problems or is your position different?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN RADINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't think he ever managed to completely solve those problems, and these problems were a serious burden for him. As far as his relation to the political authorities is concerned, he had problems with high-level politics, that is to say, with the presidency of Republika Srpska, but similarly he had problems with local politicians. I personally came across a document in which General Galic responded -- answered the complaint from the command of the general staff with regard to some of the measures he had taken in relation to the political organs of Republika Srpska. And the last sentence in that document, when he says "if anyone thinks that I have not behaved appropriately, then I have violated the rules. I consider this to be my last report", and it seemed as if he was offering his resignation. But in the army this is not a rule and it is not unusual for people to resign. But you could see from that document that he had serious problems in communicating with the high political echelons.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. General, I'll show you documents 268, 209, and 1862.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Ms. Pilipovic, I'm running into the same difficulties at this stage. I don't have numbers on all the documents. Could you provide a little guidance, please. I have 268 and 209.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] 1862, document 1862.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Yes. But I don't have any numbers on my -- on the copies provided to me, not all the numbers.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I apologise. It's document 1862, and the date is the 26th of March, 1994.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: General, do you have in front of you documents 1862, 268, and 209?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN RADINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You said that in one of the documents the general also offered his resignation. Is that document 1862?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN RADINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Let me just have a look.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Page 2 of this document, does it say that "if I have failed to respect the laws of Republika Srpska and by waging the war and leading the unit have caused damage to the Serbian people, then let this report be the last one as the report of the commander of VRS"?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN RADINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. This is the document I was referring to. And in the last paragraph, it appears that the general is offering his resignation.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: General, is that a document which was sent to the main staff of the Army of Republika Srpska and to General Milovanovic personally?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN RADINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And this document, is it apparent that this is a problem with regard to the disposition of the UNPROFOR forces in the zone of responsibility of the SRK?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN RADINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. General, from this document, can we conclude from it that the general had problems also regarding the disposition and orders to do with the work of UNPROFOR?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN RADINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. He had some serious problems there, and for many reasons. First of all, the communication with UNPROFOR was reduced by the main staff, and he had the obligation to work with them but he couldn't decide because the decision-making process was with the main staff. He couldn't make decisions. So he was here between this gap, trying to deal with UNPROFOR correctly. And on the other hand, there was also the interests of high politics and obligations of the main staff. And the way he dealt with UNPROFOR was severely restricted by the main staff.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. General, during my examination I'd like to show you a set of documents, and then my co-counsel will continue the examination. In your report you dealt in detail with the issue of UNPROFOR cooperation. Can you tell us whether General Galic took measures and what kind of measures did he take in terms of UNPROFOR cooperation?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN RADINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In looking at the documents, analysing documents for my report, I came across many documents in which General Galic is dealing with UNPROFOR issues, either ordering measures to his subordinates on how to behave with UNPROFOR personnel or ordering measures in order to protect UNPROFOR checkpoints from firing from his own forces or filing protests or responding to protests. I even came across a very warm-hearted letter written by an UNPROFOR member addressing General Galic before the UNPROFOR member left and thanking him for the support that he gave him during his mandate. I believe that was Mole.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes, General. I believe that that was mentioned in your report. Other documents now, 203, 1863, 1864, and 1865.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Ms. Pilipovic, none of my documents have any numbers on them any more. Can you please give some further guidance, dates, perhaps, of the documents.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Let's have a break. Let's have a break and let all the documents be numbered perhaps by your assistant. It's useless to -- we will adjourn until twenty minutes to 1.00. And meanwhile, may all the documents be numbered, at least the ones that -- for the registrar. If she would then read out whenever a document is shown to the witness what is the number and what is the date of that document. We'll adjourn for 20 minutes.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Mr. President, the English booth would like to make a correction.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, please do so.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: On page 48, line 22, in reference to document 264, while the witness was commenting on the content of the document, he did not say that the troops should severely treat civilians, non-Serb civilians, but that the behaviour of the troops should be strictly regulated in their behaviour towards them.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you very much for this correction for the transcript. I'd like to add that in view of the speed in which we are working at this moment, that I really admire you that you have only one correction to be made. Then I take it, Mr. Ierace, that the problems with -- well, problems -- that all issues in respect of the exhibits to be tendered through Mr. Gray are solved. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Mr. President, in terms of the Prosecution exhibits of a video nature, yes. At a stage convenient to you, I wish to say something in relation to a Defence video exhibit, that's D348/30. That's the Defence compilation video.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Madam Registrar, if you would proceed in such a way that exhibits not yet tendered, that you mention them and that we'll give an opportunity to the parties.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Perhaps before that happens, I should indicate that the Prosecution seeks to withdraw the following three videos and replace them with one, which contains all of the segments and the three to be withdrawn. Would you wish me to put them on the record right now. The three to be withdrawn are P3793, P3794, and P3798. The replacement video is P3793A. And I should add that one segment from those videos has been not placed on P3793A because it was not shown to the Court.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. I take it that Defence has received a copy -- not yet.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Not yet, Mr. President. It took all this morning to produce one copy, which Madam Registrar has now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: No, I don't. I do not have a copy.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, Mr. President. As usual, we have not received whatsoever. I would like to thank the interpreters but would like to say that we -- this is something that we wanted to tell -- to inform you about, and it's in reference to document 264. So there was a wrong meaning. And there is another thing, but in order not to slow things down, in reference to what the Prosecution has said, we have confirmed, but our position a priori is the same one, that is, that only segments of the tapes tendered should be tendered in terms of evidence and not all of the tapes. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I do understand that the Prosecution now has prepared one tape on which those fragments shown are -- do appear. So therefore, I do not know whether I truly understand your objection.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, Mr. President. We understood the same thing, and our understanding is perfectly correct, we believe. What I'm saying is that I did not view the tape. No one has viewed the tape. And I fear that in it there could be some segments that the Prosecution did not show to us during public hearing, so somehow there is something that we are trying to -- or they are trying to put under the table, so to speak. So I think that that would be something too much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Let me first look at the compilation tape. Then we can see whether there's a basis for your suspicions.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, as I can see that the Prosecution is not responding. Perhaps they could just tell us yes or no, whether they've also included the segments, which is a lot simpler, that the Prosecution wanted to tender but that they did not view in the courtroom. And then we can see what the position of the parties is.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I took it - but if I'm wrong in my understanding, Mr. Ierace, please tell me - I took it that those parts played are put on the compilation video, nothing else, nothing less. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: That's the case, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Ierace. Then would the Defence like to first view the video, or shall we take a decision on admission and then give an opportunity, if there's any -- okay. We'll then -- no, I would rather do it for one practical reason, one very practical reason, I would like to do it the other way around. As you know, sometimes we have admitted documents, exhibits into evidence, and having given an opportunity to one of the parties to come with a later objection if they had checked some items. Since we have another registrar next week, I'd rather proceed in this way today. And apart from that, Mr. Ierace has confirmed to us that there's nothing else on that tape. So to start with, we'll accept that, having not heard any specified reasons why that would not be true. But if you have checked, the Defence always has an opportunity to come back to it and object against the exhibit, that videotape. Madam Registrar. Yes, Mr. Piletta-Zanin.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] So that I can understand things fully, so the tape -- the Prosecution put on one tape also what we have played to your Chamber, or just the segments that the Prosecution had viewed?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I understood that you prepared a tape on which all the -- I think there were nine fragments -- appear that you showed, and the Prosecution has done the same, as far as I understand, for those fragments shown by the Prosecution. Madam Registrar, would you please guide us through the ...

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: P3793A, videotape containing various clips; D1845, map of Sarajevo marked by witness; D1846, UNPROFOR letter dated 29 July 1992; D1847, agreement by the Serbian Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina with regard to the opening of Sarajevo airport; D348/20, videotape containing various clips; P3788, excerpt from book written by Lewis MacKenzie entitled "Peacekeeper, the road to Sarajevo"; P3793.1, English transcript; P3794.1, English transcript; P3797, excerpt from book entitled "In harm's way"; P3787, article published by magazine, Washington report, July/August 1993; P3793.6, English transcript; P3793.2, English transcript; P3793.3, English transcript; P3793.4, English transcript; P3793.5, English transcript; P3793.7, English transcript; and P3793.9, English transcript.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Piletta-Zanin.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, it seems to be, but that is a problem, when we are working about something that has gone by, and it was some time ago. We were not able to check this, that in referring to the book by Mr. MacKenzie, this was just read out. This is not something that was handed over to us, and certainly not in the Serbian language, as it should have been done. So I believe that the Prosecution has read it well. It's all in the transcript. But this should not be tendered as an exhibit because -- I mean, as far as I recall, it was just a reading of one page or perhaps two pages, because now I recall this was a bottom of one page, and as far as I can see it in my memory now, there was a few lines in the following page of the text, so I don't think that this is something that should be tendered as an exhibit. However, Mr. President, of course my memory could fail me, and sometimes Defence has these failings.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Admitting the document into evidence would enable the Defence to find the context in which it is published. The relevant part that has been read has been translated at that very moment in a language General Galic understands. I don't know whether the Prosecution insists on tendering this document or that the objection would ...

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Mr. President, I suppose the main benefit of the tender is that it makes clear what edition the passage came from. There would be a page number at the top. Certainly the Defence was provided with a copy of the English text, but I wouldn't regard it as a critical issue. It would simply be useful for that reason.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, I object to that. I can remember that there are very interesting things for the Defence in fact in this document, so it can be tendered.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Oh.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Then all the documents are admitted into evidence, and the Defence will have an opportunity to make objections against the completeness or incompleteness of the video tendered by the Prosecution, that is, 3793A. But perhaps I had not given you an opportunity yet to make any objection, Mr. Ierace.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Thank you for that opportunity, Mr. President. It relates to Defence Exhibit D348/20. That was the Defence video compilation. The first segment was of the BBC type. It contained, amongst other things, by way of identification, three images: One of a Ukrainian radar unit, according to the commentary; some people in a forest talking about the distance to the enemy's confrontation line; and also, some words spoken by Richard Gray himself. Mr. President, I think that was shown to the witness on the first day of his testimony, which was the 18th of February. And you may recall that immediately following it being shown to the witness, I rose to my feet and questioned where on the four videotapes that particular segment had come from. And indeed that became a topic which I raised at various times over the last two and a half weeks, and the Defence indicated with assurance initially that it had come off the four videotapes which they said they received from the witness and which they disclosed to the Defence. Well, Mr. President, I have now meticulously checked the four videotapes. Each is four hours long. And that segment does not appear anywhere on the four tapes. You may remember that Richard Gray gave evidence that he gave the Defence four or five videotapes. One possible explanation is that there was indeed a fifth videotape. Mr. President, at a meeting during the week, I asked the Defence to show us where on the four videotapes the segment was, and they declined. My submission at this stage is, firstly, that the -- that segment be removed from evidence, the transcript in relation to it should remain. But more importantly, the Defence now is obliged to provide an explanation to the Trial Chamber as to where that segment came from, because the issue goes, I think even more importantly, beyond admissibility, but rather disclosure. The Prosecution would be very interested to know, if there was a fifth videotape, what else was on it. Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Piletta-Zanin or Ms. Pilipovic, could you respond to that briefly.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I know that we had a meeting about this, but I really don't know which segment it is. We were never told which was the segment in question. Can we please first resolve this issue. We, as far as I recall, we proposed to our learned colleagues if we can have a look at the segment again. I'm afraid I'm not very technically minded so that I can assess this.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Mr. President, there can be no doubt about the segment, because I rose to my feet when it was first shown to the witness. I have repeatedly referred to it as the first segment on the Defence tape.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. So it's the first segment on the Defence tape, Ms. Pilipovic, and especially there were three -- I do understand that these are three very brief passages where people are in a wood and -- yes, I remember that, although -- so it should be possible to look -- you have -- I take it you have a copy of your -- the tape you tendered into evidence. So please try to check that first --

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, we do have this tape, but on the first segment I really cannot rewind my memory to that. I'll have to have a look at it again, together with my co-counsel. But at this very moment, I really cannot recall.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. So please do then look at it again and -- Yes, Mr. Piletta-Zanin.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Mr. President. I remember very clearly this segment. In fact, I think that I can see what happened. We have to view these tapes again. We are going to try and do that during the weekend. In any case, what I do not wish to happen, for whatever -- whosever fault this is, it could have been a technical fault because there were many tapes sent back and forth. So I hope that this was -- the segment was not erased. We will have a look at our copy, because we only have copies, and of course if we can be of assistance, to the Prosecution, we will do it of course. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I'd like to hear from the Defence at the beginning of next week, either that they found the segments Mr. Ierace was referring to on one of the four tapes and where it could be found. I then think that if I would be Defence counsel and I found them, I would not be very happy after this weekend. Let me be very clear on that. If, on the other hand, it is not found, I can imagine that Mr. Ierace looking back through the hours he spent on meticulously reviewing the tapes might not be very happy. And then, of course, the next issue, whether there has been a fifth tape and whether it has been disclosed or should have been disclosed is then -- might then become an issue.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: If the parties could work on the basis of their copies. If that would create any problem, the originals have not yet been sent back to Mr. Gray, neither is the original tape that has been tendered by the Defence as being in the hands of the registrar for all this time. So if the parties -- at this moment, if the Defence would work on the basis of the copies they have, and if there's any reason to doubt whether the copies are true copies of the original, it can be checked. But then the Chamber would very much like to know exactly what parts to play and whether it has to be done in court or outside court. That's also another matter. Having said this, I think the -- most of the problems in respect of the exhibits introduced through --

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'm sorry, but I think there could be a problem in terms of my memory. These were two different segments; first, where we saw Colonel Gray at the end of one segment next to a radar where he was saying I think that if they had wanted it, they could have destroyed the --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Piletta-Zanin, just as you will need 16 hours, although by quickly viewing it it might take less hours, to look at the tape over the weekend, I'd like the Prosecution to check whether it's really at the beginning of the first fragment or not. You have got a copy. So it's a short tape. If you play it quickly, you can easily identify it. If it would be on any other place than at the beginning of the first segment, please immediately inform the Defence.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. I think as a matter of fact we are now dealing with a lot of practical problems --

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very simply, in my mind I think there are two segment, not one segment. I would just like the Prosecution to let me know. It's very brief. Are they talking about one segment or two segments? Because in the text they're only talking about one segment. It's a very simple question of clarification.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I think in the transcript you are even talk about three short --

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Three particular images, whether it's one segment or two is only known to the person who placed it on the tape. But to emphasise my point, none of those three scenes appear on any of the four tapes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. So we're talking about that. You check whether it's in the beginning of the first fragment shown in this court. If not, you immediately inform the Defence. The Defence checks over the weekend where these images could be found on one of the four original tapes, and I think we spent now enough time on it. If there's any further question in respect to this, the --

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. After court time. I mean, these are really practical problems, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No. But I didn't raise the problem, but I can answer this question very briefly so that we can sort this out. As far as I recall, yes, these are the first two segments. And I confirmed this according to my memory. And during the weekend, I will make sure that I can confirm this. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. I think the -- what is on these images has been described by Mr. Ierace, and that -- yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Mr. President, just before we return to the witness --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I would have one other issue as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I don't know whether it would be the same or not. The -- we would still hear from the Defence about whether they -- whether the subpoena issue still stands. There is a motion, either it's withdrawn or --

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: [Previous interpretation continues] ...

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Mr. President. I tried on many occasions repeatedly, and before some time ago managed to contact the wife of General MacKenzie. Now I'm only coming across his answering machine, so we have lost contact, I'm afraid.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. But the question was: There is a motion pending --

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The answer is yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: You insist on the decision.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We will bring our reply at the end of the hearing today. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. As I was saying, Mr. President, the answer is yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: You insist on a decision on the motion in which you apply for a subpoena to be issued in --

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The answer is yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. And the question -- would you please listen to me. The question to which your answer is yes is whether the Defence insists on a decision in respect of a motion they filed in which they apply for a subpoena to be issued in respect of Mr. MacKenzie? That's the first. And the other person would be Mr. Nambiar.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The answer is yes for the first part and also for the second also yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. A decision will be taken soon.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Any other issue?

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Mr. President, just in relation to rebuttal. There's a 92 bis mission in Sarajevo which is finishing on this weekend, and on Monday, if you require it, I should be able to give an update on -- give some more detail in relation to that, and certainly on Monday I expect to be able to disclose some material to the Defence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. So I take it that there will be a request to be allowed to present rebuttal evidence. Do you have any idea on how much time --

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Yes. Yes, I could assist.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: If you could give us an indication already or --

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Mr. President, at this stage there are some eight 92 bis statements. Three of them go to the destruction of mosques in Sarajevo in the indictment period. A fourth concerns the school of theology, the manner and timing of the assumption of control of the school of theology by Bosnian Serb forces, the layout of the building, its appearance when it was recovered by its usual occupants. There will be two 92 bis statements in relation to the positions of weaponry of the ABiH in the vicinity of Kosevo Hospital and the Ciglane tunnel. There will be one 92 bis statements in relation to Witness G's injury and his medical records. There will be a 92 bis statement in relation to a tape recording. If I could leave it at that at this stage, but not involving the accused. Roelof From, who is the mapping expert for the Prosecution, we will seek to call, and through him introduce five maps in respect of particular sniping incidents where the Defence has for the first time challenged whether there was a line of sight and through him also we'll seek to tender maps in relation to the balance of the sniping incidents which have the corrected latitude and longitude lines, if I could call them that. There'll be no other changes. That would simply allow one to apply a ruler to the maps. Mr. President, there are two, perhaps three, other witnesses who would be called, an investigator to give evidence in relation to the SRK documents, what he's learnt from the Defence, since that's become an issue, and perhaps Mr. Philipps in relation to issues arising from the present witness -- perhaps one or two other issues. All that in mind, Mr. President, assuming hypothetically that there was no objection -- well, I'll amend that. Assuming hypothetically that the 92 bis witnesses were accepted without the requirement for cross-examination, we would be left with, I expect, three viva voce witnesses whose evidence in chief in terms of two would be relatively short, in terms of Mr. From would ideally involve the witness from the witness box demonstrating electronically some aspects of the mapping. That would take about two hours in chief. All up, the Prosecution case, examination and cross-examination, should be less than a week if the 92 bis witnesses, any of them, are required for either examination in chief or cross-examination, that would take an extra, I should think, week and a half. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Piletta-Zanin.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, at the moment the Defence can't comment at all, but we would have appreciated it if -- may I continue?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: [Previous interpretation continues] ... Comment on it at this very moment. But yes, you would appreciate what?

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Nor do I, Mr. President. But I find it strange that we are now told about such a great number of elements that are to be provided pursuant to Rule 92 bis, and I would like to say that in my opinion it's the obligation of the Prosecution to inform us of this a lot earlier so that we can prepare for this. How are we to make our position clear if we are not at all aware of all of these facts? This is a game that the Defence does not appreciate. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. This comment doesn't add anything to --

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Mr. President, if I could respond --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: -- The issues that are in front of us. I always ask to refrain from using words like "games," et cetera, et cetera. It would have been enough to say that the Defence is surprised that it's informed this late. The Chamber has ruled when the Prosecution should give the information. They have done that. And that's it for the moment of course. At the later stage the Defence will have an opportunity to respond after they have taken knowledge of the material. Mr. Mundis.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Mr. President, if I could briefly. This -- as the Chamber is aware, the Prosecution has repeatedly sought access to the notes which this expert witness took in interviewing individuals. He made reference to passing over the bundles of his notes to the Defence in response to questions from the Bench he indicated that those notes were not taken under any form of confidentiality and that those notes are in the possession -- apparently in the possession of the Defence, with the exception of the two sets of notes that fell out of the bundle, those two having been given this morning to Madam Registrar. The Prosecution reiterates its request for copies of those notes, whether they're in the hands of the Defence or in the hands still of the expert. The Prosecution is not in a position to commence cross-examination until we have all of these notes and until these notes have been translated and until I've been given an opportunity to analyse the contents. Our position has been clear that we believe this expert has co-mingled information obtained from these interviews, many of these interviews concerned individuals who either testified - for example, the two witnesses whose notes were passed over this morning testified in this court, in this Trial Chamber in mid-January - and the Prosecution's position is clear that we believe that we are entitled to these, they go to the transparency of the expert's statement, they go to the methodology that he employed, and we believe that fairness dictates that we be given access to these notes, and it appears now that they are in the hands of Defence and that they perhaps have been for some time. And we reiterate that we want those notes, Mr. President, and we want ample time to have those notes translated and analysed before we commence our cross-examination of this expert.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Are these notes in the hands of the Defence, Ms. Pilipovic?

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, as far as I know, those notes were disclosed pursuant to the decision of the Trial Chamber. They were disclosed to the Prosecution a month ago when the Trial Chamber decided that the notes used by Mr. Radinovic for his statement -- when the decision was taken that they should be disclosed, we disclosed them. So I don't know what the problem is. I think that General Radinovic also spoke to experts on two occasions, and he didn't provide us with information on this. This was even sent from Belgrade, because I was at the trial here. I've been here from the 5th of January.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: [Previous interpretation continues] ... The Defence. The answer is they are, but they are disclosed. Mr. Mundis.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Mr. President, it appears from the expert's statement that he interviewed approximately 34 individuals, if you tally up the categories that he cites to. I believe it's page 6 of his report. We have received from the Defence notes with respect to nine of those 34 individuals.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We'll then ask the witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Thank you. And with the two that we've received today, Mr. President, that is 11 out of 34.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: For the information of the parties and -- or rather, for the Victims and Witnesses Unit, the examination of the witness will not be resumed today. So the witness is to be called in for one second so that we can instruct him as usually and tell him that we'll continue next Wednesday. So Madam Usher -- Yes, Mr. Mundis.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Mr. President, if he could also be asked about any notes, and if we could get those to begin the process of translating them, if they exist.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. I'll ask him about the notes. But that's the only thing we'll deal with. But then at the same time, next week we'll deal with all the outstanding exhibits. There's a small list. It will be given to the parties, and we will, apart from one of them - that's Exhibit D185A - introduced on the request of the Chamber by the witness Vorobev we'll take a position on that and it will be distributed to the parties, even in the absence of ...

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, I would like some information. Why next Wednesday?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Next Wednesday? I said next Monday, I think.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: You said next Wednesday. I'm asking for --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Then I apologise for this mistake.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: That's all right. That's all right.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: General Radinovic, unfortunately we see no opportunity to continue today. There would be 15 minutes left and we have to deal with a few other issues before the weekend. So we'll continue next Monday at 9.00 in this same courtroom. I again, would like to instruct you not to speak with anyone about your testimony and -- still to be given and the testimony you gave until now. I'll provide you with a small dictation machine if you promise me that you'll return it so that you can read the notes you have provided. But I have another question: Until now, your report speaks about interviews of many, many persons. Do you -- did you make notes of all these interviews? There are a little bit over 30, I think, mentioned.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, Mr. President. I spoke to some individuals on several occasions with General Lugonja, I don't know how many times I spoke to him. With General Lizdek on several occasions too.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Let me just stop you. We have received until now nine notes of interviews. There were another two provided to us today. Are these 11 sets of notes, are these the complete notes you have made of these interviews, more than 30 interviews? Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. That is clear. Then you are excused. Madam Usher, would you please escort the witness out of the courtroom.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: If there's no other urgent matter which should be dealt with right away, the Chamber would prefer to adjourn until next Monday, 9.00. We'll adjourn until next Monday, 9.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: at 1.30 p.m., to be reconvened on Monday, the 10th day of March, 2003, at 1.30 p.m. 17 18 19 20 21 22 23 24 25
